title: A Aftermath for the Silence
premise: Dominic Villalobos, a night librarian drifting through a sleepless city, is asked by Ezequiel Iriarte — the last fluent speaker of Kavilé, a dying language — to become his final student. As Dominic learns the language, he discovers it carries the testimony of a massacre the city has spent decades burying, and that Ezequiel's own survival depended on a silence he can no longer bear. When developers move to demolish the archive where the recordings are kept, Dominic must choose between legal channels that will fail and an act of public restitution outside the law: broadcasting the recordings during the city's centennial ceremony. In the end, Ezequiel dies mid-lesson, and Dominic delivers the eulogy in Kavilé — his first and last full speech in the language — saying goodbye properly, out loud, as the city finally listens.
about_author: Mara Coldharbour is the pen name of a former archivist who spent six years cataloguing endangered-language recordings before turning to fiction. She writes from a coastal apartment full of unlabeled cassette tapes and insists every novel begin with a voice that is about to be lost.

chapters.title: The Hours Between
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. Establishes his nocturnal routine at the Meridian Branch Library, his estrangement from his family, and the city's worsening insomnia. A quiet, melancholic beat: a man living like a tenant in his own life, waiting for something to claim him.

chapters.title: The Man Who Waited for Closing
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. An old man appears three nights running, reading a grammar of a language Dominic has never heard of, always leaving before dawn. On the third night he introduces himself as Ezequiel Iriarte and asks for one final student. Beat: reluctant curiosity.

chapters.title: Kavilé
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. First lesson in the library basement; Ezequiel explains Kavilé has no word for 'goodbye,' only phrases meaning 'until the sound returns.' Dominic learns his first twelve words. Emotional beat: the strange intimacy of being chosen by a dying tongue.

chapters.title: What the Tapes Remember
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. Ezequiel reveals boxes of reel-to-reel recordings in the archive — songs, names, court testimony recorded in 1971 by a priest before the massacre at Río Seco. Beat: dread beneath wonder; history pressing through the floorboards.

chapters.title: A Tenant of His Own Name
chapters.summary: POV Dominic, flashback woven in. His grandmother hummed a melody he now recognizes on tape as Kavilé; she never told him why. He calls his mother and hangs up twice. Beat: identity cracking open — he may be descended from the silenced.

chapters.title: The Demolition Notice
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. The city posts notice: the Meridian Branch will be razed for the Centennial Plaza project; archives have ninety days to relocate or be destroyed. Beat: the clock starts; quiet institutional violence rendered in bureaucratic prose.

chapters.title: Petitions and Paper Ghosts
chapters.summary: POV alternating Dominic and a young city clerk, Ana Reyes. Dominic files preservation requests; Ana processes them into oblivion. Her chapters reveal the plaza's corporate backers. Beat: justice inside the law shown as a maze designed to exhaust.

chapters.title: Until the Sound Returns
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. Lessons intensify; Ezequiel's health falters. He teaches the phrase for testimony: 'I was there, and the river saw me.' Beat: tenderness and urgency braided together; Dominic begins dreaming in Kavilé.

chapters.title: The Priest's Last Letter
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. Among the tapes they find Father Almeyda's unsent letter naming the soldiers and the officials who ordered Río Seco. Ezequiel goes silent for two days. Beat: the weight of evidence no court ever wanted.

chapters.title: Ana's Compromise
chapters.summary: POV Ana Reyes. She quietly copies the demolition file and slips Dominic the name of the developer's lawyer — her small rebellion, costing her a promotion. Beat: complicity and courage in a minor character; the law's insiders are also trapped.

chapters.title: Ninety Days, Fifty-Nine Left
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. Legal appeal denied on a technicality; the archive's contents deemed 'non-circulating materials of negligible value.' Ezequiel laughs until he coughs blood. Beat: despair sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Lesson That Wasn't a Lesson
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. Ezequiel confesses: he survived the massacre because he hid and stayed silent while others were taken; his fluency is built on that silence. He asks Dominic to promise the language will be spoken publicly, not just preserved. Beat: guilt transmuted into inheritance.

chapters.title: Plans Made After Midnight
chapters.summary: POV alternating Dominic and Ana. They plan to hijack the Centennial Ceremony's PA system with the recordings and the letter. Ana provides the broadcast schedule; Dominic rehearses the Kavilé opening. Beat: conspiracy as an act of love; fear held at arm's length.

chapters.title: What We Owe the Dead
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. A moral argument with Marisol, the head librarian, who begs him not to destroy his life over 'old tapes.' He answers that the tapes are people. Beat: the cost made explicit — job, freedom, safety all wagered.

chapters.title: Ezequiel's Decline
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. Hospital visits; lessons move to the bedside. Ezequiel drills him on the eulogy form, the kavarai, meant to be spoken only once, aloud, by someone who truly knew the dead. Beat: mortality pacing alongside the countdown.

chapters.title: Thirty-One Days
chapters.summary: POV Ana Reyes. Security tightens around the ceremony; Ana realizes she'll be on duty inside the hall. She must decide whether to be a saboteur or look away. Beat: rising tension; her arc pivots toward sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Rehearsal
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. Full run-through in the empty basement: tape decks wired to a portable transmitter, the letter scanned, the eulogy half-memorized. Something breaks; they fix it. Beat: fragile competence, the calm before catastrophe.

chapters.title: The Night Before
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. Ezequiel is hospitalized permanently; doctors say days. He makes Dominic promise to speak even if he dies before the ceremony. Dominic sits with him all night speaking Kavilé until dawn. Beat: grief and vow fused; the goodbye begins here.

chapters.title: Centennial
chapters.summary: POV alternating Dominic and Ana. Climax. During the mayor's address, Ana cuts the feed and Dominic broadcasts the Río Seco recordings across the plaza — names, songs, the priest's letter read aloud in two languages. Police close in as the crowd goes still, then weeps. Beat: catharsis at maximum risk.

chapters.title: Aftermath for the Silence
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. Arrested, charged, briefly jailed; but the broadcast went viral, the demolition is suspended, and a commission on Río Seco convenes. Charges dropped under public pressure. Beat: justice achieved outside the law, its price paid anyway.

chapters.title: The River Saw Me
chapters.summary: POV Dominic. Ezequiel dies on a Tuesday. At the funeral, Dominic rises and delivers the kavarai entirely in Kavilé — imperfect, halting, complete. The room does not understand the words and understands everything. Beat: the promised goodbye, said properly, out loud.

chapters.title: Until the Sound Returns
chapters.summary: POV Dominic, coda. Months later: the Meridian stands repurposed as a language house; Ana teaches children the first words; Dominic records himself nightly so the archive grows instead of shrinks. Final line echoes Ezequiel's phrase. Beat: quiet renewal — survival as continuation, not escape.
